text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over several years, and many people experience very mild or no early symptoms.
snippet_highlighted_words: very mild or no early symptoms

list.snippet: Frequent urination: Needing to go to the bathroom more often, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out excess sugar.
Increased thirst: Feeling unusually thirsty or dry-mouthed because fluid loss from frequent urination leaves you dehydrated.
Persistent fatigue: Feeling overly tired or weak because your body's cells cannot properly use glucose for energy.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar causing fluid to shift and swell the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing cuts or sores: Poor circulation and a weakened immune response slowing down your body's ability to repair skin damage.
Tingling or numbness: Early nerve irritation or damage (neuropathy) causing pins and needles or loss of feeling in the hands or feet.
Unexplained weight loss: Losing weight without trying as your body burns muscle and fat for fuel.
Darkened skin patches: Velvety, dark patches of skin (acanthosis nigricans) in body folds like the neck, armpits, or groin, which can signal insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Recurring urinary tract infections, yeast infections, or skin sores.

text_blocks.snippet: Because early signs can be subtle or easy to miss, doctors confirm type 2 diabetes using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic or your primary care provider:

list.snippet: A1C test: Measures your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher indicates diabetes).
Fasting plasma glucose test: Checks your blood sugar after an 8-hour fast (126 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
Random plasma glucose test: Checks your blood sugar at any time of day (200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes).
